title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
content:
About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches
cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking
English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young
children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their
shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the
women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican
Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and
had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more
recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been
abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this
informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

I'm a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in
Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because
we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how
[the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made
life more perilous for victims of domestic
abuse](https://www.propublica.org/article/domestic-violence-immigrant-victims-
ice-detention). While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we
wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic
abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner
or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and
even deported?

That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a
year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her
today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal
immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great.

None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive
partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But
they were too afraid to even leave their homes.

![Two young children — a toddler standing on the left and an older girl
sitting cross-legged on the right — with their hands pressed against large
glass exit doors looking out on a bright, leafy outdoor
area.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/PP_GrandRapidMI_DV_031_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Children
play while their relatives take part in the support group. Jamie Kelter Davis
for ProPublica

After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the
facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they
said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if
E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that
she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes.

We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on
speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it
was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we
wanted to ask. Then we began the interview.

E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out
unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at
the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d
interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been
arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence
calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported.

For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in
silence.

When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she
said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she
belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money
she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over.

A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has
been "verbally and financially abusive" and has threatened to take away the
child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn't
physically abusive.

For help in [English](https://www.thehotline.org/) or
[Spanish](https://espanol.thehotline.org/), call the National Domestic
Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

(Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview
her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take
away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed
attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When
available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement
and immigration court.)

E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she
said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal,
alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive.

That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva,
had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,”
she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already
here.”

We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse.
Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers
will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me
as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind
up losing is me.”

When we reached out to federal officials for our story, White House
spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst
of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives
have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the U.S.
Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never
apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” As
part of our reporting, we examined the backgrounds of the women we
interviewed. Most had no criminal records we could find.  

![A woman with glasses and highlighted hair wearing a black blazer over a pink
patterned dress sits attentively in a pink armchair in a warmly lit
room.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/PP_GrandRapidMI_DV_039_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=527)Angelica
Ferrer, a victim witness coordinator for Kent County Prosecutor's Office Jamie
Kelter Davis for ProPublica

People in law enforcement and the prosecutor’s office in Kent County told us
that they wanted everybody to feel safe reaching out to report crimes,
regardless of their immigration status. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker
said that he and a Spanish-speaking assistant prosecutor met with local
advocates for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence “to try and
lower that barrier, to make people understand that we see them as victims and
want to serve them as victims.”

“But,” he added, “we can talk all we want, and still, I think it’s still
difficult.”

Indeed, Angelica Ferrer, the victim witness coordinator in Becker’s office,
said she used to be able to tell victims that if they came to court, “we’re
not going to have ICE here.” She doesn’t say that to them anymore. “That is a
choice that you have to make,” she said. “I can’t guarantee that you won’t be
stopped on the way to court.”

Providing support for immigrants who are domestic abuse victims has long been
extraordinarily difficult. But over five months of reporting, Melissa and I
kept coming up against the same pervasive fear: In the current climate, nobody
can really keep them safe.

![A woman with short curly hair and glasses sits at a dark wooden dining table
and sorts through a stack of yellow cards spread out in front of her. She is
seated in a cozy home interior with a potted plant on the table, patterned
upholstered chairs and a wooden staircase rising in the background.
](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/PP_GrandRapidMI_DV_073_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=527)Mary
Sue Stegehuis folds prayer cards for people held at the North Lake Processing
Center in her home in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Jamie Kelter Davis for
ProPublica

Yet we heard from a lot of folks in Kent County who are trying to reach people
like E., whether from positions in law enforcement, via social service
agencies or as volunteers. Mary Sue Stegehuis, a retired teacher, is involved
with a grassroots group called Hope for Neighbors. Even though she doesn’t
know Spanish, she visits women in ICE custody, usually with a bilingual
friend, and she stays in touch with them through a messaging app. She prints
their stories — many involving domestic abuse — on homemade prayer cards, with
an image of Mary, Joseph and Jesus migrating from Egypt on one side. Sharing
the cards with others in the community, she told us, is meant to ensure that
their stories don’t disappear, even if the women aren’t in the room to tell
them.

We are still reporting on immigration and domestic abuse. If you have a tip or
expertise, or you just want to share something you know, please get in touch.
I’m at 313-310-6592, on both cell and Signal, and
[anna.clark@propublica.org](mailto:anna.clark@propublica.org), and Melissa is
at 872-444-0011, on both cell and Signal, and
[melissa.sanchez@propublica.org](mailto:melissa.sanchez@propublica.org).

The post [If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be
Deported?](https://www.propublica.org/article/immigration-domestic-violence)
appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
